Excerpt: If we look at the progress of computing in the 30 years before Moore wrote his article, we can chart the gains in processing power from the 1 cycle per second of Konrad Zuse’s 1938 Z1 mechanical computer — arguably the first true programmable model with a modern architecture — to the 3MFLOPs of the 1965 CDC 6600. Even if we charitably grant the Z1 1FLOP, the gain corresponds to the doubling of compute power every 12 to 18 months during that time — similar to the rate projected by Moore for integrated circuits, but across several different physical implementations. In his book on The Singularity, Ray Kurzweil goes even further back, compiling data since 1900 and the mechanical tabulator.
Moores Law at 50: Its past and its future. (Link in comments.)

Once Moore's Law became a popular idea, did it influence the industry like a self-fulfilling prophecy? It seems like IBM takes it pretty seriously and it's almost a challenge/goal for them to stick to it.

Regardless, it's still pretty awesome.
Is Moore's Law still valid? I thought it was exponential, and thus could not continue.

After briefly perusing article and the article I posted, I've come to the conclusion that when new materials are added to decrease the size of the transistor, actual chip size, or the connections between the transistors, cost is involved. Once that happens, Moore's Law takes precedent because the cost of materials is not cheap enough (at the time they're made) when a small chip set is made (say 22 nano-meters and smaller.)

 

The only way (I think) Moore's Law disintegrates is when chemistry, atomic theory, light, or quantum computing comes into play. These four factors have different properties, when applied (and safely made,) to a central processing unit (CPU) or a SoC (System on a Chip,) then the cost of that said product, will be so cheap and so fast after each iteration, it will be hard for the theoretical Moore Law to continue.
